blocks.text: A 35-year-old woman is dizzy on standing, craves salty food and has lost weight. Her blood pressure is low, her plasma sodium is low and her plasma potassium is high. The cause is failure of her adrenal glands to make aldosterone and cortisol. One hormone's absence has upset sodium, potassium and water balance at the same time, which shows how tightly the three are linked.

blocks.markdown: Sodium (Na+) is the main cation of the extracellular fluid (ECF), and the amount of sodium in the body determines the ECF volume, because water follows sodium osmotically. Potassium (K+) is the main intracellular cation: about 98 per cent of body potassium is inside cells, held there by the sodium-potassium ATPase. Plasma K+ is typically about 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L (reference ranges vary by laboratory). Because the resting membrane potential of excitable cells depends on the K+ gradient, even small changes in plasma K+ affect nerve, skeletal muscle and especially cardiac function.

blocks.title: Aldosterone
blocks.text: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid steroid hormone made in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. It acts on the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Its main stimuli are angiotensin II (from the renin-angiotensin system, triggered by low renal perfusion or low sodium) and a direct rise in plasma potassium concentration.

blocks.caption: The kidney filters a huge sodium load and reabsorbs nearly all of it, so small changes in the fraction reabsorbed cause large changes in excretion.

blocks.title: How much sodium does the kidney reabsorb?
blocks.prompt: A healthy adult has a GFR of 180 L/day and plasma sodium of 140 mmol/L, and excretes 150 mmol of sodium in a day. Calculate the filtered sodium load and the percentage reabsorbed.

steps.text: Filtered load equals GFR times plasma concentration.

blocks.answer: About 25 200 mmol/day is filtered and about 99.4 per cent is reabsorbed. If reabsorption fell by just 1 per cent, an extra 250 mmol of sodium would be lost each day, so excretion would rise to about 400 mmol, almost three times the normal value.

blocks.markdown: **How aldosterone works.** Aldosterone enters the principal cell and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor, increasing gene expression over hours. Three effects follow: more epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the luminal membrane, more renal outer medullary potassium (ROMK) channels in the luminal membrane, and more sodium-potassium ATPase pumps in the basolateral membrane. Sodium enters from the tubular lumen through ENaC and is pumped out to the blood, making the lumen electrically negative; this negative lumen potential, together with the pumped-in potassium and the extra luminal K+ channels, drives K+ secretion into the tubular fluid. Aldosterone also stimulates hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated cells. Water follows the retained sodium (when antidiuretic hormone is present), expanding the ECF.

blocks.title: Opposite effects on sodium and potassium
blocks.text: Aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium. Excess aldosterone (for example from an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma, called primary hyperaldosteronism) causes hypertension from sodium and water retention and a low plasma potassium (hypokalaemia). Too little aldosterone (as in adrenal insufficiency) causes salt and water loss with low blood pressure and a high plasma potassium (hyperkalaemia).

blocks.markdown: **Potassium handling.** Most filtered potassium is reabsorbed before the distal nephron (in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle), so urinary potassium excretion is set mostly by **secretion** in the distal tubule and collecting duct. Secretion rises with high plasma potassium, aldosterone, and increased distal flow. Short-term control also relies on shifts between ICF and ECF: insulin and beta-2 adrenergic stimulation drive potassium into cells, whereas cell breakdown and metabolic acidosis move it out. Because the ICF pool is so large, a small fractional shift has a large effect on plasma potassium.

blocks.title: A potassium shift out of cells
blocks.prompt: A man has an ECF volume of 14 L and plasma K+ of 4.0 mmol/L. Assume the ECF potassium concentration equals plasma and that his ICF holds about 3 900 mmol of potassium. A sudden injury releases 50 mmol of potassium from damaged cells into the ECF. What is the new ECF potassium concentration, and what fraction of the ICF pool was released?

steps.text: Add the released potassium (assuming no excretion and no change in volume yet).
New concentration: divide by the ECF volume. Fraction of the ICF pool: 50 / 3 900.

blocks.answer: Plasma potassium rises from 4.0 to about 7.6 mmol/L, although only about 1.3 per cent of the intracellular potassium has moved. This is why cell damage can produce dangerous hyperkalaemia.

blocks.markdown: **Natriuretic peptides** oppose the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released from atrial myocytes when they are stretched by an increased blood volume; brain natriuretic peptide (BNP, first isolated from brain but released mainly by the ventricles) is released in response to ventricular wall stretch. They increase sodium and water excretion (**natriuresis and diuresis**) by dilating the afferent arteriole and constricting the efferent arteriole (raising GFR), by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, by inhibiting renin and aldosterone secretion, and by opposing the actions of antidiuretic hormone and angiotensin II, while also causing vasodilation. BNP is measured clinically as a marker of cardiac wall stretch in heart failure.

rows: Trigger
Low renal perfusion pressure, low sodium delivery, sympathetic activity; raised plasma K+ for aldosterone
Atrial (ANP) or ventricular (BNP) wall stretch from raised blood volume
Effect on Na+ excretion
Decreased (sodium retention)
Increased (natriuresis)
Effect on water
Retained (water follows sodium; ADH and thirst increased by angiotensin II)
Increased urine volume (diuresis)
Effect on GFR and renin
Efferent constriction by angiotensin II; renin is the start of the cascade
Raised GFR; renin and aldosterone secretion inhibited
Effect on blood pressure and vessels
Vasoconstriction; blood pressure rises
Vasodilation; blood pressure falls
blocks.caption: RAAS and natriuretic peptides are opposing arms of the control of ECF volume.

rows: Hyponatraemia (plasma sodium below about 135 mmol/L)
Excess water relative to sodium: thiazide diuretics, heart failure, cirrhosis, excess antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), adrenal insufficiency, vomiting and diarrhoea with water replacement
Fall in ECF osmolality draws water into cells, causing cerebral oedema: headache, nausea, confusion, seizures, coma, worse when it develops quickly
Hyperkalaemia (plasma potassium above about 5.5 mmol/L; thresholds vary)

Reduced renal excretion (acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, aldosterone deficiency, potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors); shift out of cells (acidosis, tissue damage, insulin deficiency); excess intake with impaired excretion
Partial depolarisation of the resting membrane potential, inactivating sodium channels: muscle weakness, conduction disturbance, ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest
blocks.caption: Hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia: causes and effects. Reference limits vary between laboratories.

blocks.markdown: **Why volume loss and adrenal insufficiency cause hyponatraemia.** Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is normally released in response to a rise in plasma osmolality, but it is also released by **non-osmotic stimuli**: a fall in effective circulating volume or arterial pressure (sensed by baroreceptors) stimulates ADH release even when plasma osmolality is low, because the body prioritises defending volume over osmolality. ADH makes the collecting duct permeable to water, so water is retained and plasma sodium is diluted. Cortisol normally restrains ADH release, so in cortisol deficiency (as in adrenal insufficiency) ADH release is increased and the kidney cannot excrete free water normally. In adrenal insufficiency, aldosterone deficiency adds renal sodium loss and volume depletion, so both mechanisms favour a low plasma sodium.

blocks.title: Sodium concentration is not sodium content
blocks.text: Plasma sodium concentration reflects the ratio of sodium to water, not total body sodium. A patient with oedema from heart failure has too much total sodium and too much water, yet may have a low plasma sodium because water excess is larger. Also, correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly can cause brain injury (osmotic demyelination), so it is a hazard to be recognised, not something to try at the bedside from a lesson.

points: Aldosterone, released in response to angiotensin II and raised plasma K+, acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct to increase Na+ reabsorption (ENaC, Na+/K+ ATPase) and K+ secretion (ROMK).
The kidney filters about 25 000 mmol of sodium a day and reabsorbs more than 99 per cent; potassium excretion is set largely by distal secretion, and ICF-ECF shifts can change plasma K+ rapidly.

Hyponatraemia causes cerebral oedema as water moves into cells and can arise when volume depletion (non-osmotic) and cortisol deficiency raise ADH; hyperkalaemia depolarises excitable cells and can cause fatal arrhythmias.
ANP and BNP, released by atrial and ventricular stretch, cause natriuresis and diuresis, raise GFR, and inhibit renin, aldosterone and ADH, so they oppose the RAAS.

questions.stem: Which effect of aldosterone on the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct is correct?

options.text: Increased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium secretion
Decreased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium secretion
Increased sodium reabsorption and decreased potassium secretion
Decreased sodium reabsorption and decreased potassium secretion

questions.correctOptionText: Increased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium secretion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aldosterone raises ENaC, ROMK and Na+/K+ ATPase activity.
distractorRationale.b: Aldosterone increases, not decreases, sodium reabsorption.
distractorRationale.c: Aldosterone increases, not decreases, potassium secretion.

questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases luminal ENaC and ROMK channels and basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase in principal cells. Sodium is therefore retained and potassium is secreted into the tubular fluid.

questions.stem: Which pair of stimuli directly increases aldosterone secretion by the adrenal zona glomerulosa?

options.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide and a fall in plasma potassium
Angiotensin II and a rise in plasma potassium concentration
Raised blood volume and raised plasma sodium
Antidiuretic hormone and insulin

questions.correctOptionText: Angiotensin II and a rise in plasma potassium concentration

distractorRationale.a: ANP inhibits aldosterone secretion and a fall in plasma potassium would also reduce it.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: angiotensin II and hyperkalaemia are the main stimuli.
distractorRationale.c: A raised blood volume suppresses the renin-angiotensin system and therefore aldosterone.
distractorRationale.d: These are not the principal stimuli of aldosterone secretion.

questions.explanation: Angiotensin II, formed by the renin-angiotensin system, and a direct rise in plasma potassium both stimulate the zona glomerulosa. Natriuretic peptides and raised blood volume suppress aldosterone secretion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has persistent hypertension and a plasma potassium of 2.9 mmol/L. Investigation reveals an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. Which pair of mechanisms best explains his two findings?

options.text: Excess sodium and water retention raising blood volume, and excess potassium secretion in the distal nephron
Excess sodium loss lowering blood volume, and reduced potassium secretion
Excess sodium and water retention raising blood volume, and reduced potassium secretion
Excess sodium loss lowering blood volume, and excess potassium secretion

questions.correctOptionText: Excess sodium and water retention raising blood volume, and excess potassium secretion in the distal nephron

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aldosterone retains sodium (raising blood volume and pressure) and drives potassium secretion, causing hypokalaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Aldosterone excess retains, not loses, sodium and increases potassium secretion.
distractorRationale.c: The sodium effect is right, but aldosterone increases potassium secretion; reduced secretion would cause hyperkalaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Aldosterone excess retains sodium; sodium loss would occur in aldosterone deficiency.

questions.explanation: Excess aldosterone increases ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption, expanding ECF volume and raising blood pressure, and increases potassium secretion, producing hypokalaemia. The opposite pattern (low blood pressure with hyperkalaemia) is seen with aldosterone deficiency.

questions.stem: A woman has an ECF volume of 15 L and a plasma potassium of 4.8 mmol/L. After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin release drives 12 mmol of potassium from the ECF into cells. Assuming no urinary excretion, no intake and no change in ECF volume, calculate the new ECF potassium concentration in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: The initial ECF potassium is 15 x 4.8 = 72 mmol. Moving 12 mmol into cells leaves 60 mmol, and 60 / 15 = 4.0 mmol/L. This shows that insulin shifts potassium into cells and lowers plasma potassium, the reverse of the shift out of cells that occurs with tissue damage or insulin deficiency.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman becomes confused and has a generalised seizure ten days after starting a thiazide diuretic. Plasma sodium is 118 mmol/L. Which mechanism most directly explains her neurological symptoms?

options.text: Water moves into brain cells because the ECF osmolality has fallen, causing cerebral oedema
Water moves out of brain cells because ECF osmolality has risen, causing shrinkage
Potassium moves out of neurons, causing hyperpolarisation
A raised plasma sodium causes neuronal depolarisation

questions.correctOptionText: Water moves into brain cells because the ECF osmolality has fallen, causing cerebral oedema

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hyponatraemia lowers ECF osmolality, so water enters cells, including brain cells, which are confined within the skull.
distractorRationale.c: Plasma potassium is not the primary issue in the vignette.
distractorRationale.d: Plasma sodium is low, not raised.

questions.explanation: Low plasma sodium reduces the effective osmolality of the ECF, creating an osmotic gradient that moves water into cells. Brain cells swell inside the rigid skull, causing headache, confusion and seizures, particularly when the fall is rapid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause hyperkalaemia?

options.text: Acute kidney injury with very little urine output
Persistent vomiting
Treatment with a loop diuretic
Primary hyperaldosteronism

questions.correctOptionText: Acute kidney injury with very little urine output

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reduced GFR and low distal flow impair potassium excretion, causing it to accumulate.
distractorRationale.b: Vomiting tends to cause potassium loss and hypokalaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Loop diuretics increase distal flow and potassium loss, causing hypokalaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Aldosterone excess promotes potassium secretion, causing hypokalaemia.

questions.explanation: The kidney is the main route of potassium excretion, so when it fails to produce urine potassium accumulates. The other options all tend to deplete potassium.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with primary adrenal insufficiency (aldosterone deficiency) has a GFR of 100 mL/min, a plasma sodium of 130 mmol/L and a urinary sodium excretion of 600 mmol/day. Taking one day as 1440 minutes, calculate the percentage of the filtered sodium that is reabsorbed.
questions.explanation: A GFR of 100 mL/min is 144 L/day, so the filtered sodium is 144 x 130 = 18 720 mmol/day. Reabsorbed sodium is 18 720 - 600 = 18 120 mmol/day, which is 18 120 / 18 720 x 100 = 96.8 per cent. This is below the usual figure of more than 99 per cent, showing how loss of aldosterone's stimulation of ENaC and the Na+/K+ ATPase leaves more sodium to be excreted.

questions.stem: What is the principal stimulus for the release of atrial natriuretic peptide?

options.text: A fall in arterial pressure sensed at the kidney
Stretch of the atria from an expanded blood volume
A rise in plasma potassium
Increased plasma osmolality

questions.correctOptionText: Stretch of the atria from an expanded blood volume

distractorRationale.a: A fall in renal perfusion stimulates renin release, the opposite arm.
distractorRationale.c: Raised potassium stimulates aldosterone, not ANP.
distractorRationale.d: Raised osmolality stimulates ADH release, not ANP.

questions.explanation: ANP is stored in atrial myocytes and released when they are stretched by increased central blood volume. Its actions promote natriuresis and diuresis, helping to reduce that volume.

questions.stem: Outline how the natriuretic peptides oppose the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in the control of sodium and water balance.
markingGuide: ANP is released from atrial myocytes on stretch (BNP from ventricles) in response to increased blood volume
They increase GFR by dilating the afferent and constricting the efferent arteriole
They inhibit sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, causing natriuresis and diuresis
They inhibit renin release and aldosterone secretion
They oppose the actions of angiotensin II and antidiuretic hormone and cause vasodilation
States that the RAAS acts in the opposite direction, retaining sodium and water and raising blood pressure
questions.explanation: Natriuretic peptides respond to stretch from excess volume by promoting sodium and water excretion and suppressing renin and aldosterone, thereby opposing the RAAS. The two systems thus form complementary arms that adjust ECF volume up or down.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency has low blood pressure, plasma sodium of 124 mmol/L and plasma potassium of 5.9 mmol/L. Explain each of these findings in terms of the actions of aldosterone, and state the main danger of the potassium level.
markingGuide: Aldosterone normally increases sodium reabsorption (ENaC, Na+/K+ ATPase) in the late distal tubule and collecting duct
Deficiency causes urinary sodium and water loss, a lower ECF volume and low blood pressure

Hyponatraemia results from sodium loss with relative water retention: volume depletion stimulates non-osmotic ADH release, and cortisol deficiency (which normally restrains ADH) further raises ADH release and impairs free water excretion
Aldosterone normally promotes potassium secretion, so deficiency reduces potassium excretion and causes hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia partially depolarises the resting membrane potential, impairing excitability and conduction
Danger: cardiac arrhythmias including ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest, and muscle weakness
questions.explanation: Without aldosterone, the distal nephron reabsorbs less sodium and secretes less potassium, so sodium and water are lost and potassium is retained. Volume depletion and cortisol deficiency raise ADH, which retains water and dilutes plasma sodium. The resulting hyperkalaemia depolarises excitable membranes and threatens cardiac rhythm, which is why it is the most dangerous of her electrolyte changes.
